summary:
Consensual, private, non-commercial same-sex sexual activity between adults has been lawful in Guatemala since 1871.

Guatemala provides no legal gender recognition. Since 2016 a person may change a legal name to match gender identity only with judicial permission; legal gender cannot be changed, and a person cannot self-report gender for official documents, which must show the sex and name assigned at birth. The resulting mismatch between presentation and identity documents exposes a trans visitor to scrutiny during identity checks.

Guatemala is bound by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion OC-24/17 of 9 January 2018, which holds recognition of gender identity on official documents to be a human right under the American Convention on Human Rights and requires states parties to grant same-sex couples access to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage with all rights deriving from marriage.

Legislative movement on recognition has gone in the opposite direction. A December 2017 bill to recognise the right to gender identity and allow transgender people to change name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by both the Legislative and Constitutional Points Commission and the Women's Commission, and later proposals for a gender identity law permitting change of official documents have been advocated without enactment.

Initiative No. 5940, received by the Legislative Directorate on 12 July 2021 and presented to the plenary of the Congress of Guatemala on 13 September 2021, proposes a law to guarantee the integral protection of children and adolescents against gender identity disorders and was assigned to the Human Rights, Education, Science and Technology, and Governance commissions. Bill 5490, advanced in December 2021, would remove education regarding transgender individuals in schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents from "gender identity disorders" and require censorship of media featuring transgender individuals; it was unanimously approved by the Congress's Education, Science and Technology committee and moved for full congress review.

Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations such as cafes, restaurants, nightclubs and cinemas. A May 2017 bill to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category remains unadopted, and the penal code's prohibition of discrimination on grounds including gender does not explicitly cover gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. No convictions for discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds were recorded through 2021.

Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of gender identity are reportedly tolerated by the Guatemalan government, particularly where harassment or violence is directed at transgender people, and the absence of hate-crime protection is attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles.

Trans women are held in men's prisons on birth-sex placement. A 2020 Human Rights Watch report documents that practice and the resulting sexual assault, recording no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice and no court ruling on trans custody. Bárbara Herrarte of Redmmutrans described her time in a men's prison: "Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him." The same reporting flags forced internal displacement of LGBT people from violence.

Conversion practices operate openly, mainly through Evangelical-funded centres in rural areas, and include electroshock therapy, forced marriage and coerced sex; "corrective" rape is prosecuted only as rape and not as a hate crime. Such practices remain normalised, including among mental health professionals.

Documented violence is longstanding. United Nations and NGO reports from the late 1990s recorded systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a social cleansing campaign, including the 1997 gunning down in Guatemala City of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia. Central American governments have long excluded trans women from femicide protections, and Guatemalan officials have justified that exclusion by stating that transgender women are not "biological women".

There is no legal recognition for same-sex couples as marriage, civil union or domestic partnership. A civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by Deputy Sandra Morán has not been debated since. The Protection of Life and Family initiative (5272), which would increase penalties for abortion, explicitly ban same-sex marriage, define family as "being a father, a mother and children" and describe homosexuality as "being contrary to biology and genetics", passed first and second readings in 2018 with its third reading blocked that September. Congress approved the law again on 8 March 2022; after President Alejandro Giammattei announced a veto on grounds it violated the Constitution and international agreements, Congress archived and discarded it on 15 March 2022 by 119 votes, leaving its prohibitions without effect.

An opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash against gender recognition in Guatemala and neighbouring jurisdictions. In August 2025 the Guatemalan Congress hosted the Meeting for Religious Freedom, Life and Family to advance an anti-LGBTIQ agenda, and despite the election of a more progressive government in 2024 the legislature remained predominantly conservative with no significant pro-LGBTIQ initiatives.
tangentialFactors:
Guatemala's social climate reflects its religious composition: a majority of Guatemalans affiliate with the Catholic Church or Pentecostal churches, and these traditions have upheld socially conservative positions, tending to treat homosexuality and cross-dressing as signs of immorality. The same attitudes are reflected in the dominant political parties, while most smaller parties generally ignore LGBT rights.

Openly LGBT political representation began with lesbian Deputy Sandra Morán elected in January 2016 and gay Deputy Aldo Dávila elected in June 2019, both on platforms to criminalise hate crimes and hate speech against the LGBT community. Former President Álvaro Colom supported civil unions, while President Jimmy Morales supported the marriage ban proposal, stating that Guatemala believes in a family based on the marriage of a man and a woman.

The Arcus Foundation reported in May 2024 that the Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, with binary-framed opposition generating backlash in all four countries.

Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations, apart from a 1997 Code on Childhood and Youth safeguard that was repealed in 2003; a May 2017 bill to add sexual orientation to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 remains unadopted.

Visibility has grown since the 1990s: OASIS was permitted in 1993 to provide HIV/AIDS education and expanded to LGBT rights after the 1996 end of the civil war, and the first gay pride parade was held in Guatemala City in 2000. Only one gay bar was allowed from 1976 until the late 1990s, against a rising fundamentalist Pentecostal population.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot self-report gender for official government documents, which must show gender and name assigned at birth. The resulting document mismatch causes problems accessing government services such as education and basic resources that require official identification.

Guatemalan law provides no protection against discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations, and no convictions on those grounds were recorded through 2021.

Transgender residents in custody are placed in men's prisons on birth-sex basis with no gender-identity placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice and no court ruling on trans custody, a configuration documented in 2020 as facilitating sexual assault.

Conversion practices, including electroshock therapy, forced marriage and coerced sex, continue through Evangelical-funded centres mainly in rural areas and are normalised among mental health professionals; "corrective" rape is prosecuted only as rape. Attempts to ban educational materials on transgender identities have persisted, and the 1997 safeguard for children and youth against discrimination based on sexual orientation was repealed in 2003.
outOfScopeNotes:
Guatemala's compliance with the Inter-American Court's advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 is not recorded in the available sources, so the gap between the opinion's requirements and practice on document recognition and couple recognition remains unresolved.

The sources carry no trans-specific killing rate for Guatemala and no denominator against which such a figure could be read, so no comparative magnitude of trans homicide risk can be stated. Reported incidents are described qualitatively rather than as rates.

The status of Bill 5490 and Initiative No. 5940 beyond their 2021 committee and plenary stages is not sourced, and whether either was enacted, archived or withdrawn is unresolved.

No sourced material addresses airport or border screening of gender presentation, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or facilities and restroom rules for visitors; these are not covered rather than absent.

Whether the government elected in 2024 altered any policy on gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection is not documented in the inventory.
